_about: Plain-English voter guide: one card per party contesting the 2026 party vote. Written to the same template and standard for every party. Facts are dated and sourced; 'they_say' is the party's own framing and 'critics_say' is attributed criticism, neither is the archive's view. polling_avg_2026 and track_record_line are filled in by tools/guide_enrich.py from data/polls-2026.json and data/promises/*.json. Policy ids point to parties/<slug>/policies/policies.json (policy.nz POL ids or archive-assigned ids); minor parties not covered by policy.nz cite their own documents instead.
party_count_note: 17 parties are registered with the Electoral Commission for the 2026 election and can contest the party vote (RNZ, 12 Oct 2026; Electoral Commission register). All 17 appear on policy.nz's 2026 party-vote list.
position_method: 'position' is the left-right label in the party's English Wikipedia infobox (retrieved 23 Oct 2026). Where Wikipedia gives no position label we say so and quote how the article describes the party instead. Labels are Wikipedia's, not ours.

parties.name: New Zealand National Party
parties.tagline: The largest party in Parliament, leading the current government, promising no new taxes and a return to surplus.
parties.in_a_nutshell: National leads the government now, with ACT and NZ First. It wants to keep taxes where they are, cut government debt and get the books back in surplus. It is promising compulsory KiwiSaver, longer paid parental leave and tougher sentencing for some crimes.

big_ideas.text: No new taxes next term, and the government's books back in surplus by 2028/29
Make KiwiSaver compulsory for workers and sign babies up at birth
Split Foodstuffs (New World, Pak'nSave, Four Square) into two separate companies to boost supermarket competition
Extend paid parental leave from 26 to 30 weeks
More money for medicines (Pharmac) and free bowel screening from age 50, paid for partly by cutting foreign aid outside the Pacific
Replace NCEA, make students finish Year 11, and limit screen time for young children at school
Tougher justice rules: no 'good character' sentence discounts for sex offending and a clear 'yes' needed for consent

they_say.text: National's slogan is "Fixing the Basics, Building the Future"; its fiscal plan says a re-elected National government will "not impose new taxes" and will "return to surplus in 2028/29 and stay there".
they_say.attribution: National Party (fiscal plan, 12 Oct 2026; slogan as reported by policy.nz)

critics_say.text: Labour says "National promised to grow the economy and get the Government's finances in order. It has done neither - unemployment is higher, growth is weaker, debt has continued to rise, and frontline services have been cut."

current_seats.note: 48 won at the 2023 election, plus Port Waikato, won at the November 2023 by-election (Wikipedia election article, 'Current seats').

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Led the government since November 2023 (with ACT and NZ First) and from 2008 to 2017.
parties.track_record_line: Led the government since November 2023 (with ACT and NZ First) and from 2008 to 2017. Of 71 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 35 kept, 11 partly kept, 5 broken, 10 abandoned, 10 still in progress. (11 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Wants to continue the current government with ACT and NZ First. Luxon ruled out a 'grand coalition' with Labour (May 2026) and formally ruled out any deal with Opportunity, including confidence and supply, from 27 July 2026, citing its plans to raise taxes; he repeated this through October.

costings.summary: Yes. Its fiscal plan (12 Oct 2026) keeps new spending to $2.4b a year, leaves $7.5b of operating money unallocated over four years, and part-funds promises by cutting foreign aid. It includes $1.2m for an election policy costings unit.

parties.name: New Zealand Labour Party
parties.tagline: The main opposition party, campaigning on cheaper doctors' visits paid for by a capital gains tax on property.
parties.in_a_nutshell: Labour is the biggest opposition party and last governed from 2017 to 2023. It wants three free GP visits a year, paid for by a new tax on profits from selling property (not the family home). It also promises to restore pay equity and take on big companies over prices.

big_ideas.text: Up to three free GP visits a year, paid for by a 28% capital gains tax on property sales (family homes excluded)
Free prescriptions, free cervical screening for ages 25-69 and free referred maternity scans
Restore the old pay-equity law and give 65,000 care and support workers a $4 an hour pay rise
Make price gouging illegal and force the supermarket giants to separate their wholesale and retail businesses
Cap public transport fares at $20 a week in the three biggest cities ($10 elsewhere) and freeze fuel tax for three years
A 'NZ Future Fund' to invest in New Zealand businesses and infrastructure
Wipe 10% off eligible graduates' student loans and build at least 6,000 more social homes

they_say.text: Labour's slogan is "Better Starts Now". It says "every promise Labour has made is fully paid for" and that it "will balance the books without shrinking the economy".

critics_say.text: National's Nicola Willis called Labour's fiscal plan fraudulent, saying Treasury estimates restoring the old pay-equity scheme would cost $11 billion, leaving Labour about $8.5 billion short; Labour says it has enough unallocated money and won't name a figure during negotiations.
critics_say.attribution: Nicola Willis, National finance spokesperson (via RNZ)

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Led governments from 1999 to 2008 and 2017 to 2023; in opposition since 2023.
parties.track_record_line: Led governments from 1999 to 2008 and 2017 to 2023; in opposition since 2023. Of 71 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 36 kept, 10 partly kept, 7 broken, 18 abandoned. (21 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Will keep working with the Greens and says its 'door is open' to Opportunity. It has ruled out NZ First (formally, 10 Aug 2026) and ACT. It says it could work with Te Pāti Māori but senior roles for them are 'unlikely', and Hipkins ruled out giving the Greens or Te Pāti Māori the police or corrections portfolios (14 Oct 2026). Its campaign chair says his preference is a government with just the Greens and Opportunity.

costings.summary: Yes. Its fiscal plan (Oct 2026), reviewed by accounting firm Hall Chadwick, keeps the $2.4b operating allowance, forecasts a surplus in 2028/29 and aims for net debt below 20% of GDP. National disputes how pay equity, fuel tax and the Future Fund are accounted for.

parties.name: Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand
parties.tagline: An environmental and social-justice party proposing new taxes on the very wealthy to fund public services.
parties.in_a_nutshell: The Greens want strong action on climate change and nature, and more help for people on low incomes. They would tax people with more than $10 million in wealth and cut income tax for most workers. They also want a government-owned supermarket and limits on rent rises.

big_ideas.text: A 2.5% yearly tax on wealth above $10 million and a tax on large inheritances and gifts, so most workers can get an income tax cut (first $10,000 tax-free)
Cap rent rises at 2% a year and build many more public homes
'KiwiMart': force the supermarket giants to sell 120 stores to a new government-owned chain
Free public transport for children, students, apprentices and Community Services Card holders, and $2 fares for everyone else
A new publicly owned company, 'Kiwipower', to build renewable energy
An extra $3 billion a year for health, and restore pay equity for care workers
Keep and expand free school lunches and make early childhood education free

they_say.text: The Greens' slogan is "For All of Us". Co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick says the government's current budget path is "made possible only through underinvestment in core public services".
they_say.attribution: Green Party; Chlöe Swarbrick (fiscal plan launch, 23 Oct 2026)

critics_say.text: National's campaign chair Simeon Brown says the Greens' plan contains "nine new taxes"; the Greens' own fiscal plan shows net core Crown debt about $26.6 billion higher than Treasury's forecast by 2030/31.
critics_say.attribution: Simeon Brown, National (via B2B News); Green fiscal plan figures

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Never a full coalition partner; supported Labour-led governments in 2017-2020 (confidence and supply, with ministers outside Cabinet) and 2020-2023 (cooperation agreement).
parties.track_record_line: Never a full coalition partner; supported Labour-led governments in 2017-2020 (confidence and supply, with ministers outside Cabinet) and 2020-2023 (cooperation agreement). Of 22 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 11 kept, 4 partly kept, 6 broken, 1 abandoned. (10 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Campaigning to change the government with Labour: the two parties held a joint stand-up at Waitangi in February 2026 to show they would work together. Co-leader Marama Davidson said the Greens had stayed in contact with Te Pāti Māori through its internal troubles. We found no formal Green statement this campaign ruling other parties in or out.
coalition_stance_2026.note: We found no explicit Green statement on working with Opportunity, National, ACT or NZ First.

costings.summary: Yes. Its fiscal plan (23 Oct 2026), with direct fiscal effects reviewed by Infometrics, raises about $28.75b over four years from new taxes, lifts yearly new spending to $4.5-4.7b, delays surplus to 2029/30, and has net core Crown debt reaching $256.4b (44% of GDP) by 2030/31.

parties.name: ACT New Zealand
parties.tagline: A free-market party in the current government that wants a smaller state and lower government spending.
parties.in_a_nutshell: ACT is part of the current government with National and NZ First. It wants the government to spend less, have fewer ministries and treat everyone the same regardless of race. It would slowly raise the pension age to 67 and scrap the net-zero climate law.

big_ideas.text: A smaller government: merge 43 departments into 19 and abolish ministries for particular groups (such as women, Pacific peoples and ethnic communities)
Raise the pension (NZ Super) age gradually to 67 by 2035
Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and the net-zero target, and abolish the Climate Change Commission
Freeze the minimum wage for three years and bring in a lower training wage
Three strikes for burglary and deporting serious offenders who aren't citizens
Let pharmacists treat more illnesses and lift Pharmac's share of the health budget
Remove ethnicity-based criteria from public services and close the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are settled

they_say.text: ACT says "New Zealand needs a smaller, more efficient government if we are going to balance the books, lift wages, restore trust in democracy, and unlock New Zealand's potential."
they_say.attribution: ACT New Zealand ('A Smaller, More Affordable Government')

critics_say.text: The Greens called ACT's fiscal plan "welfare for the wealthiest" and Labour accused ACT of "punching down", after it proposed raising the pension age and spending $653 million less on disability benefits.
critics_say.attribution: Green Party and Labour Party (via RNZ)

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: In coalition government with National and NZ First since 2023; supported National-led governments 2008-2017.
parties.track_record_line: In coalition government with National and NZ First since 2023; supported National-led governments 2008-2017. Of 33 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 18 kept, 4 partly kept, 5 broken, 6 abandoned. (5 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Wants to keep the current government and 'lock Labour out'. Seymour said a four-party deal including Opportunity, if it crossed 5%, 'would be a good outcome' to keep the Greens and Te Pāti Māori out of power (16 Oct 2026). Labour has ruled ACT out.

costings.summary: Yes. Its fiscal plan (11 Oct 2026) promises lower debt and spending, including raising the pension age by three months a year and $653m less on disability benefits. RNZ noted two items (about $100m a year, and tax relief of $264m-$303m a year) were not explained.

parties.name: New Zealand First

position.label: no position label in Wikipedia infobox
position.description: Wikipedia's opening sentence calls it a "right-wing populist" party; the infobox lists right-wing populism, nationalism and social conservatism as its ideology.
position.note: Wikipedia editors have not agreed a position label

parties.tagline: A party led by Winston Peters, in the current government, focused on citizens-first policies and breaking up big companies.
parties.in_a_nutshell: NZ First is part of the current government and has been in government with both Labour and National in the past. It wants some benefits, like the pension and voting, kept for citizens only. It also wants to break up the big power companies and buy back the BNZ bank.

big_ideas.text: Split the big power companies' generation and retail businesses
Split Foodstuffs into two cooperatives and give the Commerce Commission more power
Buy back the Bank of New Zealand (BNZ) into public ownership
Only citizens could vote and get NZ Super; citizens first for social housing
A $5,000-a-year 'Kiwi Kids Grant' for a child's first three years, and $70 a week more Working for Families tax credit
Cut company tax to 20% for small and medium businesses
A binding referendum on the Māori seats and replacing the Waitangi Tribunal with a completion commission

they_say.text: Winston Peters says "what is needed more than anything else is serious skill, and serious experience in the next government" and that "It is vital that the left does not win."

critics_say.text: The NZ Herald reports NZ First is the largest party in Parliament not publishing a fiscal plan; a Green Party analysis put its policies at about $71.6 billion over four years, which NZ First rejects without giving its own figures. Labour's Chris Hipkins accused the party of "overt racism" when ruling it out.
critics_say.attribution: NZ Herald; Green Party; Chris Hipkins (Labour)

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: In government four times: with National (1996-98, 2023-26) and with Labour (confidence and supply 2005-08, coalition 2017-20).
parties.track_record_line: In government four times: with National (1996-98, 2023-26) and with Labour (confidence and supply 2005-08, coalition 2017-20). Of 43 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 21 kept, 3 partly kept, 7 broken, 9 abandoned, 3 still in progress. (7 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Has repeatedly ruled out Labour. At the TVNZ multi-party debate Peters said he could work with 'the parties in government now' (National and ACT), and after the Herald debate (21 Oct 2026) said 'No, I can't' when asked if he could sit at a Cabinet table with Opportunity's Qiulae Wong. Labour has also ruled NZ First out.

costings.summary: No full fiscal plan. The NZ Herald (23 Oct 2026) says NZ First is the largest party in Parliament not publishing one. It has costed some items itself, e.g. about $1b a year for the small-business tax cut and $7.5b to buy back the BNZ (other estimates are as high as $24b).

parties.name: Te Pāti Māori
parties.tagline: A Māori rights party asking Māori-roll voters for their electorate vote, focused on Te Tiriti and Māori self-determination.
parties.in_a_nutshell: Te Pāti Māori wants Māori to have more say over their own lives and resources, based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Its plan is to win the Māori electorate seats and to get people to give their party vote to Labour or the Greens. It would make the first $30,000 of income tax-free and add a wealth tax.

big_ideas.text: 'Kiwi Tax Plan': first $30,000 of income tax-free, a wealth tax, and a higher company tax rate
Take GST off food (kai)
An independent Te Tiriti Commission and binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations
Work towards a new constitution based on Matike Mai, and put the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples into practice
Abolish prisons by 2040, replacing them with community-led solutions
A $1 billion fund for Māori and community ownership of renewable energy
A Māori Education Authority to run Māori education

they_say.text: Co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "There's one plan, two votes" and "The only way we're going to get this government out, get more Māori in Parliament, and continue to be the loudest, unapologetic, independent Māori voice is to focus on giving our votes to Te Pāti Māori candidates."
they_say.attribution: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer (campaign launch, 16 Aug 2026, via RNZ)

critics_say.text: Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said Te Pāti Māori needs to "prove themselves to the country that they are worthy of being part of a government", after a year in which the party split and expelled two MPs.

current_seats.note: Won 6 electorates in 2023; MPs Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Tākuta Ferris were expelled in Nov 2025 (Kapa-Kingi now leads the Te Tai Tokerau Party; Ferris sits as an independent).

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Supported National-led governments under confidence-and-supply deals from 2008 to 2017 (as the Māori Party); in opposition since 2020.
parties.track_record_line: Supported National-led governments under confidence-and-supply deals from 2008 to 2017 (as the Māori Party); in opposition since 2020. Of 15 past promises checked in this archive's tracker: 8 kept, 3 partly kept, 3 broken, 1 abandoned. (6 2026 promises are tracked but not yet due.)

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Wants to remove the current government and asks supporters to give their party vote to the 'left bloc' (Labour or the Greens). Responding to Labour saying senior roles were 'unlikely', co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said "Te Pāti Māori will have that conversation on 8th November."
coalition_stance_2026.note: 'rules_out' reflects its stated aim to remove the current government; we found no formal rule-out statement worded as such.

costings.summary: No full fiscal plan found. It published a 'Kiwi Tax Plan' (26 Aug 2026) setting out new taxes and rebates, but we found no published overall costing of its spending promises.

parties.name: Opportunity Party
parties.tagline: A centrist party, polling near or above 5%, proposing a land tax to fund a regular 'Citizen's Income' payment.
parties.in_a_nutshell: Opportunity has never been in Parliament, but polls suggest it could get in and decide who governs. Its big idea is a weekly 'Citizen's Income' for most adults, paid for by a tax on land. It also wants to clean up political donations and lobbying and ban bottom trawling.

big_ideas.text: A 'Citizen's Income' of up to $370 a week for most adults, funded by a land value tax
Clean up politics: cap donations at $30,000, a lobbying register and an anti-corruption watchdog
A 10-year plan for the health system, lifting health funding to 9% of GDP
Phase out inshore bottom trawling by 2030 and protect 30% of the ocean
Give the Commerce Commission more teeth against monopolies and duopolies
Bring farming into the emissions trading scheme and build a $5b climate-resilience fund
Make public transport free

they_say.text: Leader Qiulae Wong says Opportunity would be an MMP kingmaker that is an "accelerator for progress - instead of a handbrake on change".
they_say.attribution: Qiulae Wong (State of the Nation speech, Feb 2026, via Scoop)

critics_say.text: National's Christopher Luxon said Opportunity's universal income "wants to make every New Zealander a beneficiary" and its land tax "is going to be massive"; commentator Grant Duncan argues its claimed $4b-a-year surplus is largely offset by new borrowing costs.
critics_say.attribution: Christopher Luxon (via RNZ, 27 Jul 2026); Grant Duncan (Substack)

polling_avg_2026.method: Simple mean of all 9 published party-vote polls with fieldwork ending in the 30 days to 2026-10-23 (no weighting).

parties.track_record_context: Has never had an MP, so has no record in Parliament; its best result was 2.4% in 2017.
parties.track_record_line: Has never had an MP, so has no record in Parliament; its best result was 2.4% in 2017.

coalition_stance_2026.summary: Says it will talk to either side and will 'pick up the phone' to National if it is the largest party, but "we are not here to prop up the current coalition government" and would not support a Treaty Principles bill. It has ruled out a government with Winston Peters as Foreign Minister, and set five bottom lines (Commerce Commission powers, lobbying and donations reform, a 10-year health plan, phasing out bottom trawling, and Paris Agreement commitments).
coalition_stance_2026.conditions: No government with Winston Peters as Foreign Minister; five bottom lines.
coalition_stance_2026.note: RNZ (27 Jul 2026) reported the party 'has been open to working with both National and Labour'. We found no explicit statement about the Greens or Te Pāti Māori.

costings.summary: No full fiscal plan found. Its 'Tax Reset' policy says that, on 2024 numbers, the land value tax pays for the Citizen's Income with about $4b a year left over; independent commentators dispute parts of this.

parties.name: New Zealand Loyal

position.label: far-right
position.note: Wikipedia infobox; Wikipedia lists the leadership as disputed between Kelvyn Alp and founder Liz Gunn

parties.tagline: A small party that wants New Zealand out of the UN, WHO and WEF and opposes climate agreements.
parties.in_a_nutshell: NZ Loyal was started in 2023 by Liz Gunn and is now led by Kelvyn Alp. It wants New Zealand to leave international bodies like the UN and WHO and drop climate agreements. It got 1.2% of the party vote in 2023.

big_ideas.text: End New Zealand's participation in the UN, the World Economic Forum and the World Health Organization
End climate agreements and pursue energy independence, including oil and gas
Scrap the current tax system
Scrap all race-based policies and write a New Zealand constitution
Decentralise government and 'return power to the people'

they_say.text: "We reject government overreach. We take our country back from foreign interests. We restore our freedoms. No compromise. No apologies."
they_say.attribution: NZ Loyal website, as quoted by RNZ

critics_say.text: RNZ notes that leader Kelvyn Alp was arrested and charged with sharing the livestream of the 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks, and is a founder of the Counterspin platform, which RNZ describes as far-right.

polling_avg_2026.method: Not reported separately in the main public polls (pollsters group it under "other"). policy.nz lists its 2026 polling average as <0.5%.

parties.track_record_context: Has never had an MP; won 1.21% of the party vote in 2023. It was deregistered in July 2024 and re-registered on 5 August 2026.
parties.track_record_line: Has never had an MP; won 1.21% of the party vote in 2023. It was deregistered in July 2024 and re-registered on 5 August 2026.

coalition_stance_2026.summary: No public statement on post-election partners found.

parties.notes: The party website could not be retrieved for this archive (see parties/nz-loyal/policies/documents/nzloyal-com-not-retrievable.md); policies are taken from RNZ's quotation of it.

parties.name: NZ Outdoors & Freedom Party

position.label: no position label in Wikipedia infobox
position.description: Wikipedia says its "policies combine environmentalism with anti-government conspiracy theories"; its listed ideology includes anti-1080, environmentalism and anti-vaccination.

parties.tagline: A small party, now calling itself 'freedom', focused on individual rights, direct democracy and outdoor access.
parties.in_a_nutshell: This party began as the NZ Outdoors Party and grew after opposing COVID-19 vaccine mandates. It wants the Bill of Rights to become supreme law so governments can't override it. It also opposes 1080 poison and wants better public access to the outdoors.

big_ideas.text: Make the NZ Bill of Rights 'supreme law' that no future government can override
Direct democracy: let citizens decide laws through binding votes
Replace the Department of Conservation with a new 'Department of Outdoors' promoting access, recreation and food gathering
Natural ecosystems free from poisons such as 1080
Speed up house building by freeing land and revising resource-management rules

they_say.text: "People hold the power. You choose the laws. Join the global movement striving for Direct Democracy."
they_say.attribution: Party website, as quoted by RNZ

critics_say.text: After a group of the party's anti-vaccination activists (as Wikipedia's election article describes them) confronted Labour MP Ayesha Verrall at a Wellington candidates' meeting (8 Sept 2026), Labour leader Chris Hipkins said "some people had strong anti-science views and they did not represent the vast bulk of New Zealanders".

polling_avg_2026.method: Not reported separately in the main public polls (pollsters group it under "other"). policy.nz lists its 2026 polling average as <0.5%.

parties.track_record_context: Has never had an MP; in 2023 it stood under the Freedoms NZ umbrella, which won 0.34%.
parties.track_record_line: Has never had an MP; in 2023 it stood under the Freedoms NZ umbrella, which won 0.34%.

coalition_stance_2026.summary: No public statement on post-election partners found.

parties.name: Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis Party

position.label: no position label in Wikipedia infobox
position.description: Wikipedia describes it as "dedicated to the legalisation of cannabis for medical, recreational and industrial use".

parties.tagline: A single-issue party that wants cannabis legalised and regulated for medical, recreational and industrial use.
parties.in_a_nutshell: The Cannabis Party has stood at every election since 1996 but has never won a seat. It wants adults to be able to grow and use cannabis without being prosecuted. It would also clear past cannabis convictions and grow a hemp industry.

big_ideas.text: Stop prosecuting adults for possessing, growing and using cannabis
Regulated R18 cannabis sales, like alcohol and tobacco but with no advertising
Wipe all past cannabis convictions
Allow medicinal cannabis and full-scale hemp farming
Overhaul the Misuse of Drugs Act

they_say.text: "ALCP exists to legalise, regulate, and normalise cannabis for medicinal, recreational, and industrial use, while reducing harm caused by prohibition."
they_say.attribution: Party website, as quoted by RNZ

critics_say.text: We found no prominent named criticism of the party in 2026 campaign coverage. For context, voters narrowly rejected legalising recreational cannabis in the 2020 referendum.
critics_say.attribution: Archive note; Electoral Commission referendum result

polling_avg_2026.method: Not reported separately in the main public polls (pollsters group it under "other"). policy.nz lists its 2026 polling average as <0.5%.

parties.track_record_context: Has never had an MP; won 0.45% of the party vote in 2023.
parties.track_record_line: Has never had an MP; won 0.45% of the party vote in 2023.

coalition_stance_2026.summary: No public statement on post-election partners found.

parties.name: Animal Justice Party Aotearoa New Zealand

position.label: no position label in Wikipedia infobox
position.description: Wikipedia says it "advocates non-violence towards animals, sustainability, and a move away from animal-based agriculture".

parties.tagline: A small party focused on animal welfare and a gradual shift away from animal farming.
parties.in_a_nutshell: The Animal Justice Party wants animals to be treated with respect and protected by law. It wants to end factory farming, with help for farmers to switch to plant-based food or other land uses. It also wants no-kill dog pounds and an independent Commissioner for Animals.

big_ideas.text: End factory farming and ban the most harmful farming and fishing practices, with funded help for farmers to change
Make rehoming and 'no-kill' the national default for dog pounds
An independent Commissioner for Animals with real powers
Give animals legal standing so they are not treated simply as property
More plant-based food in schools and hospitals, and fairer access to vet care
Get money out of politics and protect whistleblowers

they_say.text: "We're here because the animals don't have a vote, and someone needs to speak up for them honestly and without apology."
they_say.attribution: Co-leaders Danette Wereta and Rob McNeil (2026 manifesto)

critics_say.text: We found no prominent named criticism of the party in 2026 campaign coverage.

polling_avg_2026.method: Not reported separately in the main public polls (pollsters group it under "other"). policy.nz lists its 2026 polling average as <0.5%.

parties.track_record_context: Has never had an MP; won 0.17% of the party vote in 2023.
parties.track_record_line: Has never had an MP; won 0.17% of the party vote in 2023.

coalition_stance_2026.summary: No public statement on post-election partners found.

parties.name: Alliance Party of Aotearoa New Zealand
parties.tagline: A democratic socialist party, back on the ballot, wanting public ownership of key services and a wealth tax.
parties.in_a_nutshell: The Alliance was in government with Labour from 1999 to 2002, then faded away, and has now come back. It wants the government to own power, rail and other key services again. It would make the first $20,000 of income tax-free, paid for by a wealth tax.

big_ideas.text: First $20,000 of income tax-free, paid for by a 2.5% wealth tax above $2 million, a capital gains tax and a financial transactions levy
'Reverse privatisation': bring electricity, telecommunications networks, rail and key ports back into public ownership
Free GP, dental, optical and hearing care through a public Community Health Service
Full employment, a 35-hour week with no loss of pay, and five weeks' annual leave
A big public house-building programme to clear the social housing waitlist, with social rents capped at 25% of income
Keep NZ Super universal at 65 and end the asset test for rest-home care

they_say.text: "We are a democratic socialist party building a fairer Aotearoa New Zealand."
they_say.attribution: Party website, as quoted by RNZ

critics_say.text: We found no prominent named criticism of the party in 2026 campaign coverage.

polling_avg_2026.method: Not reported separately in the main public polls (pollsters group it under "other"). policy.nz lists its 2026 polling average as <0.5%.

parties.track_record_context: In coalition with Labour from 1999 to 2002; out of Parliament since 2002, deregistered in 2015 and re-registered on 5 August 2026.
parties.track_record_line: In coalition with Labour from 1999 to 2002; out of Parliament since 2002, deregistered in 2015 and re-registered on 5 August 2026.

coalition_stance_2026.summary: No public statement on post-election partners found.

costings.summary: Partly. It published 'Tax Policy Costings: The Numbers' (Sept 2026) for its tax package, which it says produces a net revenue surplus; we found no costing of its full programme.

parties.name: Conservative Party NZ
parties.tagline: A socially conservative party for lower taxes, 'one law for all', and legal protection for the unborn.
parties.in_a_nutshell: The Conservatives (called New Conservatives in 2023) want smaller government and lower taxes. They oppose policies based on race or identity and want New Zealand to leave the Paris climate agreement. They also want the law to recognise an unborn child as a person from the last trimester.

big_ideas.text: Lower income and company taxes, a 12.5% GST rate, and no tax on NZ Super
'One people under one law': no policies based on race, ancestry, sex or identity
Leave the Paris Agreement and scrap climate-based taxes on fossil fuels
Legal personhood for an unborn child from the last trimester, with more support for women in crisis pregnancies
Shift visas towards skilled professionals and entrepreneurs using a stable points system
A Royal Commission of Inquiry into police performance

they_say.text: "We are working to bring a conservative voice to Parliament, to turn back the 'woke' agenda and prevailing culture of death."
they_say.attribution: Party website, as quoted by RNZ

critics_say.text: Wikipedia notes that some opponents and observers have described the party's policies as far-right; the party says it has moved to a 'more centrist' position under new leadership.

polling_avg_2026.method: Not reported separately in the main public polls (pollsters group it under "other"). policy.nz lists its 2026 polling average as <0.5%.

parties.name: Women's Rights Party

position.label: no Wikipedia article or position label
position.description: Wikipedia's 2026 election article lists its ideology as gender-critical feminism.

parties.tagline: A small party focused on women's sex-based rights, such as single-sex spaces and sport.
parties.in_a_nutshell: The Women's Rights Party was started in 2023 by two former Labour members. It says rights for women should be based on biological sex. It wants single-sex spaces for women and girls and stricter limits on medical gender treatment for young people.

big_ideas.text: Protect single-sex spaces for women and girls
Extend the ban on puberty blockers to cross-sex hormones for under-18s, and limit gender surgery to over-25s
Fair play in women's sport
Clear, plain language about women in law, health care and the media
Recognition and fair reward for women's paid and unpaid work

they_say.text: "We are women and men who believe in democracy, equality and biological reality."
they_say.attribution: Party website, as quoted by RNZ

critics_say.text: Wikipedia describes co-leader Jill Ovens as an "anti-transgender activist"; the party rejects that description and has urged supporters to stop donating to Wikipedia over it.

polling_avg_2026.method: Not reported separately in the main public polls (pollsters group it under "other"). policy.nz lists its 2026 polling average as <0.5%.

parties.name: Vision New Zealand
parties.tagline: A Christian conservative party linked to Destiny Church, focused on family values and pausing immigration.
parties.in_a_nutshell: Vision NZ is led by Hannah Tamaki of Destiny Church. It says strong families should come first and the government should do less. It wants to pause mass immigration, leave the Paris climate agreement and make the first $25,000 of income tax-free.

big_ideas.text: A Ministry for Families and a Parental Rights Bill
Make the first $25,000 of income tax-free, and stop taxing superannuation
Pause mass immigration and lengthen the wait for citizenship to 10 years
Leave the Paris Accord and suspend commitment to UN regulations
Define sex in law as male and female and ban gender-transition treatment for minors
Abolish MMP party lists so only electorate winners sit in Parliament, cut the number of MPs, and add term limits

they_say.text: "We believe that the family is the ultimate cornerstone of society and the primary incubator for our nation's morals, which is why we will dismantle state dependency, strip away government overreach and restore parental authority to its rightful place."
they_say.attribution: Party website, as quoted by RNZ

critics_say.text: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said a February 2025 Destiny Church protest that disrupted a rainbow event at an Auckland library went "too far"; Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown called the behaviour "thuggery".

polling_avg_2026.method: Not reported separately in the main public polls (pollsters group it under "other"). policy.nz lists its 2026 polling average as <0.5%.

parties.name: Free Palestine (Palestine Free from the River to the Sea Party)

position.label: no position label in Wikipedia infobox
position.description: Wikipedia lists its ideology as anti-Zionism and single-issue politics.

parties.tagline: A new single-issue party focused on Palestine and an independent foreign policy.
parties.in_a_nutshell: Free Palestine was set up in 2026 and is contesting its first election. It wants one democratic, secular state in all of historic Palestine with equal rights for everyone. It also wants New Zealand to leave military and security alliances with the United States.

big_ideas.text: A single, secular, democratic state in all of Palestine with equal citizenship
The right of return for all Palestinian refugees
Press the government to back prosecutions for war crimes and uphold UN resolutions
An independent foreign policy, withdrawing from military and security alliances with the US

they_say.text: "A political party committed to justice, international law and a democratic national state with equal rights for all citizens."

critics_say.text: The Electoral Commission received 207 submissions opposing the party's registration, some calling its name and logo offensive; it allowed the registration but refused the proposed logo, which contained a Palestinian flag.
critics_say.attribution: Electoral Commission process, reported by RNZ

parties.name: Te Tai Tokerau Party

leaders.name: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi
leaders.role: Leader, MP for Te Tai Tokerau

position.label: no position label in Wikipedia infobox
position.description: Wikipedia lists its ideology as tino rangatiratanga (Māori self-determination).

parties.tagline: A new Northland-based Māori party formed by sitting MP Mariameno Kapa-Kingi after her split from Te Pāti Māori.
parties.in_a_nutshell: This party was started in May 2026 by Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, the MP for Te Tai Tokerau, after she fell out with Te Pāti Māori. It puts children (mokopuna) and whānau wellbeing at the centre of its policies. It is standing two candidates.

big_ideas.text: A 'Mokopuna Act' requiring government to assess and report how its decisions affect children, with an independent Commissioner for Mokopuna
Wipe about $2 billion of debt that low-income whānau owe to MSD and IRD, and simplify the benefit system
A Crown-iwi fund so local mana whenua get at least a 25% stake in big regional infrastructure projects
Move money from prisons into hapū-run rehabilitation 'healing sanctuaries'
An independent, iwi-governed Māori health authority

they_say.text: "Mō ngā tamariki, mō ngā mokopuna te take. For our tamariki and mokopuna - that is the cause."
they_say.attribution: Party website, as quoted by RNZ

critics_say.text: We found no prominent named criticism of the new party itself in campaign coverage. Kapa-Kingi was expelled by Te Pāti Māori in November 2025 over accusations of financial misconduct; the High Court ruled the suspension and expulsion unlawful.

current_seats.note: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, elected for Te Pāti Māori in Te Tai Tokerau in 2023 (policy.nz lists 1 current MP).
